hints: Think about what changes in the atom as you move from $\text{Na}$ to $\text{Ar}$: what is added to the nucleus and what is added to the electron shells?
Link the increasing proton number with constant shielding from the same inner shells to the strength of pull on the outer electrons.
walkthrough:
Picture what is the same across the period**
You are moving from $\text{Na}$ to $\text{Ar}$ in the third row. Every atom is using the n = 3 shell for its outer electrons. The inner shells (1 and 2) are full and do not change much, so the shielding effect stays roughly the same.

Picture what is different**
The proton number rises one by one, from 11 in sodium to 18 in argon. That means more positive charge packed into the nucleus, with no extra inner shell to block it.

Connect stronger pull to smaller size**
With more nuclear charge and similar shielding, the effective pull on each outer electron gets stronger. The outer shell is drawn in closer to the nucleus, so the atomic radius falls across the period.

Final answer: Across Period 3 nuclear charge / proton number increases while electrons are added to the same shell, so shielding remains approximately constant.
There is greater attraction between the nucleus and the outer electrons, pulling them closer so atomic radius decreases.

hints: Write out the $3\text{p}$ electron arrangements for phosphorus ($3\text{p}^3$) and sulfur ($3\text{p}^4$) and look for singly occupied versus doubly occupied orbitals.
Think about what happens to the energy needed to remove an electron when two negatively charged electrons share the same small orbital.
walkthrough:
Compare the p electron boxes**
Phosphorus is $1\text{s}^22\text{s}^22\text{p}^63\text{s}^23\text{p}^3$. By Hund's rule its three $3\text{p}$ electrons sit one in each orbital, all unpaired. Sulfur is $...3\text{p}^4$, so the fourth electron must pair up with another in the same orbital.

Feel the repulsion in the pair**
Two electrons crowded into the same orbital repel each other strongly. That repulsion pushes the energy of that paired electron up a little, it is already less stable.

Link to ionisation energy**
First ionisation energy is the energy to remove the most easily lost electron: $$\text{S(g)} \rightarrow \text{S}^+\text{(g)} + \text{e}^-$$ Because the paired electron in sulfur is already repelled, it takes less extra energy to pull it away completely than to remove a stable unpaired electron from phosphorus.

Final answer: Sulfur has the configuration $...3\text{s}^23\text{p}^4$ with a pair of electrons in one $3\text{p}$ orbital, whereas phosphorus $...3\text{s}^23\text{p}^3$ has three singly occupied orbitals.
Electron-electron repulsion in the paired orbital in sulfur makes the electron easier to remove, so less energy is required.

hints: Recall the structure types: which of sodium and phosphorus has a giant lattice of positive ions in a sea of electrons, and which exists as discrete $\text{P}_4$ molecules?
Think about what particle must be free to move for a solid to conduct electricity.
walkthrough:
See sodium as a sea of electrons**
Sodium metal is a lattice of $\text{Na}^+$ ions surrounded by delocalised $3\text{s}$ electrons that are free to drift throughout the whole piece. When a voltage is applied, these mobile electrons flow easily, that flow is an electric current.

See phosphorus as separate molecules**
Phosphorus is made of discrete $\text{P}_4$ molecules held together only by weak van der Waals forces. All the valence electrons are locked up in strong localised covalent bonds inside each molecule.

Compare charge carriers**
Conduction needs mobile charged particles. Sodium provides them in abundance, phosphorus provides none, its electrons cannot move from molecule to molecule and there are no ions free to move. So sodium conducts well and phosphorus does not.

Final answer: Sodium has a giant metallic structure with mobile / delocalised electrons free to move and carry charge.
Phosphorus has a simple molecular / covalent structure with localised electrons and no mobile charged particles, so it is a poor conductor / insulator.

hints: Compare how many outer shell electrons each sodium atom and each magnesium atom contributes to the sea of delocalised electrons.
walkthrough:
Count the electrons each atom donates**
Both are metals with mobile electrons, so look closer. $\text{Na}$ is $[\text{Ne}]3\text{s}^1$ and gives one electron per atom to the sea. $\text{Mg}$ is $[\text{Ne}]3\text{s}^2$ and gives two electrons per atom to the sea. More free electrons per unit volume means charge can flow more easily, so magnesium is the better conductor.
Final answer: Each magnesium atom contributes two delocalised / valence electrons compared to one from each sodium atom, so more mobile charge carriers are available to conduct.

hints: Start with $\text{HNO}_3\text{(aq)} + \text{Mg(s)}$: think of this as an acid plus reactive metal reaction and decide what salt of magnesium must form in solution.
Recall what gas is always released when a reactive metal displaces hydrogen from a dilute acid.
Recall the characteristic thermal decomposition of a Group 2 nitrate to the oxide, and list the two gaseous products formed alongside $\text{MgO}$.
Use the product list $\text{MgO(s)} + \text{H}_2\text{O(g)} + \text{C(g)} + \text{D(g)}$ to assign the two nitrate decomposition gases, noting that their order does not matter.
walkthrough:
Identify A and B from metal plus acid**
Magnesium is well above hydrogen in the reactivity series, so with aqueous nitric acid it forms a magnesium salt plus hydrogen: $$\text{Mg(s)} + 2\text{HNO}_3\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{Mg(NO}_3\text{)}_2\text{(aq)} + \text{H}_2\text{(g)}$$ So solution A is magnesium nitrate, $\text{Mg(NO}_3\text{)}_2$, and gas B is hydrogen, $\text{H}_2$.

Recall how magnesium nitrate breaks up on heating**
Group 2 nitrates (except the very stable barium type) decompose on heating to the oxide plus nitrogen dioxide plus oxygen: $$2\text{Mg(NO}_3\text{)}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MgO} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$$ The water shown, $\text{H}_2\text{O(g)}$, comes from evaporation of the aqueous solution on heating.

Assign C and D**
That leaves the two decomposition gases as brown $\text{NO}_2$ and colourless $\text{O}_2$. Either box can be either gas, so C and D are $\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ in either order.

Final answer: A = $\text{Mg(NO}_3\text{)}_2$
B = $\text{H}_2$
C = $\text{NO}_2$ or $\text{O}_2$
D = $\text{O}_2$ or $\text{NO}_2$ (the other gas to C)

hints: Work backwards: a white solid that gives $\text{CO}_2$ (cloudy limewater) with acid must contain which anion, and what soluble source of that anion could precipitate $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ from solution A?
walkthrough:
Deduce E then X**
Gas that turns limewater cloudy is $\text{CO}_2$, so white solid E must be a carbonate that releases $\text{CO}_2$ with acid. Since solution A contains $\text{Mg}^{2+}$, E is $\text{MgCO}_3$. To precipitate it you need a soluble carbonate that provides $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ ions, so reagent X must be a soluble Group 1 carbonate such as $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3\text{(aq)}$ or ammonium carbonate.
Final answer: A Group 1 carbonate, e.g. $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3\text{(aq)}$ or $\text{K}_2\text{CO}_3\text{(aq)}$, or ammonium carbonate, $\text{(NH}_4\text{)}_2\text{CO}_3\text{(aq)}$
